subject: Mathematical Foundation of Generative AI
title: From variational divergence minimization to GANs
description: Start with samples and a critic, learn how a GAN takes turns, then follow a handwritten-digit training example.

intro.text: Topic 1 is available: Realization of Variational Divergence Minimization. Continue from the variational representation studied in Week 1.

sections.title: Making fake data that looks real

blocks.text: Start here Imagine a bag full of cat photos. You can take photos out, but you do not know the rule that made them. Can we build a machine that makes new cat photos that look like the ones in the bag? This page shows how.
Words you will see
• Data: the real examples we are given, like the cat photos.
• Generator: a neural network. It takes random numbers and turns them into fake data.
• Neural network: a machine made of many simple steps. Its settings are called weights. Changing the weights changes what it outputs.
• Distribution: the pattern of how likely each kind of data is.
• Divergence: one number that tells how different two patterns are. If the patterns are the same, the number is zero.
• Average: add up many values and divide by how many there are.
• Critic: a second neural network. It gives a score to the data it sees.
The setup
We have real data: x₁, x₂, …, xₙ. We do not know the rule behind it.
We build a generator. It takes random noise z (random numbers) and makes a fake sample x̂.
Our goal is simple: change the generator's weights until its fake data looks like the real data.
Everyday example A copy machine. You feed it random ink patterns. It prints pages. You adjust the machine until the printed pages look like the real pages in the bag.
Problem 1: we cannot measure the difference directly
We want a divergence number that measures how different the fake and real data are. But to compute it, we would need the full pattern of both. We do not have that. We only have samples.
Idea 1: averages of samples are enough

For each sample, first compute its score. Then add the scores and divide by the number of samples. With many independent draws from the same source, this average approaches the long-run average when the expected score is finite.

blocks.alt: A pile of samples turning into one average
blocks.caption: Many samples go in, one average comes out.

blocks.text: Idea 2: use a lower bound

We cannot compute the exact divergence. So we find a number that is always less than or equal to the divergence. We call it a lower bound. The lower bound is written using two long-run averages, one for real data and one for generated data. We estimate them from separate batches. The exact lower-bound guarantee is for the long-run averages. A particular batch estimate can overshoot the true divergence.

For each generator, first try to make the bound as tight as possible by improving the critic. Then adjust the generator to bring that critic’s score down. A weak critic can give a small score even when the distributions are far apart.

blocks.alt: The population critic score is at most the true divergence. A finite-batch estimate can exceed it.
blocks.caption: The inequality applies to the population score. The batch score estimates it.

blocks.text: Idea 3: use a second network as the critic
The lower bound has a part where we must search for the best scoring function. We cannot search over all functions. So we use a neural network, called the critic, with its own weights w.
The two goals are now:
• The generator wants the score to be small. It changes its weights θ to do this.
• The critic wants the score to be big. It changes its weights w to do this.
Each one tries to undo what the other is doing. That is why this is called an adversarial game.

blocks.alt: Noise to generator to fake sample to critic to score
blocks.caption: The generator makes a fake sample. The critic scores it against real data.

blocks.text: Worked example — turn two batches into one score
Give heads 0 points and tails 2 points. The real batch is heads, tails, tails, heads. Add its four scores and divide by four.
For a KL-based critic, convert each generated score into a penalty. Here T is the points assigned to one toss.
The generator gives four heads, so each penalty is about 0.37. Subtract their average from the real average.

blocks.alt: Real tosses heads, tails, tails, heads earn 0, 2, 2, 0 points and average 1. Four generated heads each have a penalty of about 0.37. Subtracting the averages gives about 0.63.
blocks.caption: Each average uses its own four tosses. The difference is the score for these batches.

blocks.text: Try giving both outcomes 1 point instead. Every real score and generated penalty is now 1, so the critic gets zero. The choice of scoring rule matters even when the generator stays fixed.
What is a saddle point?
Picture a horse saddle. If you walk forward, you go up. If you walk sideways, you go down. The middle point is a saddle point.

At a saddle point of the minimax game, changing only the critic cannot increase the score, and changing only the generator cannot decrease it. The diagram shows the local shape with two slices. Taking turns is a way to search for a solution, and convergence depends on the game and updates.

blocks.alt: A saddle surface with a ball in the middle, arrows up one way and down the other
blocks.caption: At a saddle, the score is locally highest when changing only the critic and locally lowest when changing only the generator.

blocks.text: The critic has a special last step
The critic must give values in the right range for the divergence we chose. So the critic has two parts:
1. A normal neural network that outputs one plain number.
2. A fixed squashing step. It turns that number into a value in the right range.
Three steps inside the critic
Think back to the coin example. The network first gives each outcome a raw number. A second rule converts that number into a score the chosen divergence can use.

Here x is the sample and w holds the critic’s weights. The raw output can be any real number. The activation puts it inside the domain where the conjugate is finite. That domain depends on the choice of divergence, which is why the last step can change.
In the next lesson, the GAN activation gives a negative final score. The GAN conjugate needs that range.
In one line
A generator makes fake data. A critic scores data. They play a game on the same score, and the generator learns to make data that the critic cannot tell apart from the real data.
Words to remember: divergence · lower bound · critic · generator · saddle point · adversarial
Practice — Quick check

Question: Why can't we measure the divergence directly? Answer: We would need the full pattern of the real and fake data. We only have samples, so we use a lower bound that we can compute from samples.
Question: What does the generator want? Answer: It wants the score to be small. It changes its weights to make the fake data look more real.
Question: What does the critic want? Answer: It wants the score to be big. It changes its weights to find the best way to tell real from fake.
Start here Last time the generator and critic shared a score. This time we’ll choose a score that lets the critic answer a familiar question. Did this sample come from the real data or the generator?
Words you will see
• Log (log): a math function. For numbers between 0 and 1, the log is negative. For example, log of 0.5 is about −0.69.
• Sigmoid: a function that turns any number into a value between 0 and 1. Big numbers go close to 1. Very small numbers go close to 0.
• Probability: a number from 0 to 1 that says how likely something is. 0.9 means "very likely".
Step 1: choose the GAN's function
The original GAN objective comes from this choice of divergence function.
Adding twice the natural log of 2 makes the function equal zero at 1. It shifts the score by a constant, so the training directions stay the same.
Step 2: the critic's score must follow a rule
Our critic gives a plain number for each sample. We must squash that number so it fits the rule of our chosen function.
For a GAN, the squashing rule is:
Here v is the plain number from the critic, and e is a special number, about 2.718.
Why does it fit? The exponential is positive, so the number inside the log is greater than 1. Its log is positive, and the minus sign makes the score negative. That is the range the conjugate needs.
Step 3: use a sigmoid to get a clear answer
We now define the discriminator. It is the critic with a sigmoid at the end:
For any finite input, D(x) lies strictly between 0 and 1. Read it as the discriminator’s estimate that the sample came from the real data.

blocks.alt: Sigmoid squeezes any number into a value between 0 and 1
blocks.caption: The values at −5 and 5 are rounded. A finite input never gives exactly 0 or 1.

blocks.text: Step 4: put it all together
The sigmoid gives the discriminator probability D. The critic score T used in the variational objective is the natural log of that probability.
The generated term subtracts the conjugate. Since exponentiating the critic score gives D back, the generated term simplifies to the log of one minus D.

blocks.tex: \begin{aligned}J={}&\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{x\sim P_X}[\log D(x)]}_{\text{average on real data}}\\&+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\hat{x}\sim P_\theta}[\log(1-D(\hat{x}))]}_{\text{average on generated data}}\end{aligned}

blocks.text: This is the GAN formula from the original paper.
What it means in words:
• For real data, we want D to be close to 1, because we want the critic to say "real".
• For fake data, we want D to be close to 0, because we want the critic to say "fake".

blocks.alt: Real samples pushing D toward 1, fake samples pushing D toward 0
blocks.caption: In the discriminator turn, real samples are the positive examples and generated samples are the negative examples.

blocks.text: A simple number check
Suppose the critic is confused and gives every sample the value D = 0.5.
• For each sample, log(0.5) is about −0.69.
• The critic cannot tell real from fake. It is guessing.
Now suppose a real sample gets D = 0.88. The critic is fairly sure it is real. That is a good sign.

Everyday example A teacher checks test papers. For a real paper, the teacher should say "yes, this is real" with high confidence. For a fake paper, the teacher should say "no". The score rewards assigning high probability to the correct source, so confidence matters too.
Why the conjugate needs a negative score

The conjugate converts the critic’s score into the generated-side penalty. For the unnormalized function above, the quantity inside its log must be positive. That requires the exponential of the score to be below 1, so the score must be negative.

The discriminator probability lies strictly between 0 and 1 for a finite raw score. Its log is therefore negative. Exponentiating the log gives D back, so subtracting the conjugate produces the second term in the GAN score.
What the best discriminator tells us

Remember how the ideal coin judge uses the best possible real-probability score for each outcome? Do that over all inputs, with the two sources equally weighted. The best achievable GAN score then measures how different the distributions are through Jensen–Shannon divergence.

Jensen–Shannon divergence is symmetric and lies between zero and the natural log of 2. If the distributions match, it is zero, and the optimal discriminator gives 0.5 for either source on the shared support. The two logs then add to minus log 4. The constant changes the baseline without changing which generator is best. A limited or partly trained discriminator can score below the theoretical optimum. Here the maximum refers to an ideal discriminator that can output 0 or 1 when appropriate.
Worked example — one prediction, two outcomes

Suppose the judge gives a heads result a real probability of 0.8. If the result was real, the judge gave the right source 0.8. If it was generated, the judge gave the right source only 0.2. The log rewards the first answer more.

blocks.alt: D is 0.8 in both cases. The real sample contributes about −0.223. The generated sample contributes about −1.609.
blocks.caption: Use the probability assigned to the true source before taking the log.

blocks.text: Why do we call D a classifier?
D always gives a value between 0 and 1. That is the same kind of answer as a yes-or-no question with a confidence level. A network that answers yes or no like this is called a classifier.
In one line
If we pick the right function, the GAN is just a critic that says "real or fake" with a number from 0 to 1.
Words to remember: sigmoid · probability · log · discriminator · classifier
Practice — Quick check
Question: What does D = 0.5 mean? Answer: The critic is not sure. It cannot tell real from fake.
Question: What should D be for a real sample? Answer: Close to 1. The critic should say "real".
Question: What is a sigmoid? Answer: A function that turns any number into a value between 0 and 1.
Start here Training a GAN is like a game with two turns. First the critic practises spotting fakes. Then the generator practises fooling the critic. Repeat many times.
Words you will see
• Batch: a small group of samples, for example 128 photos at once.
• Gradient: a direction that tells us how to change the weights to make a score go up or down.
• Going up (ascent): change the weights to make the score bigger.
• Going down (descent): change the weights to make the score smaller.
• Frozen: we do not change these weights in this turn. They stay the same.
What we start with
We start with real examples and choose networks suited to the data. A small fully connected network will do for the handwritten-digit example.
Step 1: use small groups instead of all the data
We cannot use all the data at once. So we use batches.
• Take a batch of real samples.
• Make a batch of fake samples. Make random noise, and pass it through the generator.
Step 2: the critic's turn
The critic tries to make its score bigger. Its job is to get better at spotting fakes.
1. Take a batch of real samples. Ask the critic: "real or fake?" Note how it does.
2. Take a batch of fake samples from the generator. Ask the critic again.
3. Combine the two results. Find the direction that makes the score bigger.
4. Change only the critic's weights a little, in that direction.
The generator is frozen during this turn.

Try one round with a coin. Suppose the real batch has five heads and five tails, while the generated batch has nine heads and one tail. If the judge sees a tail and knows only the outcome, five of the six matching examples came from the real coin. That makes a tail a stronger clue than a head.

blocks.alt: Five out of fourteen heads are real. Five out of six tails are real.
blocks.caption: For these two equally sized batches, the best real-probability guesses are about 36% for heads and 83% for tails.

blocks.text: Step 3: the generator's turn
The generator tries to make its score smaller. Its job is to fool the critic.
1. Make random noise. Pass it through the generator to get fake samples.
2. Ask the critic about these fake samples.
3. Find the direction that makes the score smaller.
4. Change only the generator's weights a little, in that direction.
The critic is frozen during this turn.
Key point: in the generator's turn, we do not need real data. The real-data part of the score does not depend on the generator. So it does not matter for this turn.

Now keep those two judge scores fixed. Suppose the generator adjusts its setting so tails make up 30% of its outputs instead of 10%. That replaces some low-scoring heads with higher-scoring tails. The next judge update will use fresh samples and can revise its scores.

blocks.alt: Generated tails rise from one in ten to three in ten. The judge still gives heads about 36% and tails about 83% as its real probabilities.
blocks.caption: Only the generator changes on this turn. The rows illustrate the old and new proportions.

blocks.text: A small worked example
Say we have 2 real samples and 2 fake samples. The critic gives these values:
Sample Critic's value What we use Real 1 0.9 0.9 Real 2 0.8 0.8 Fake 1 0.2 1 − 0.2 = 0.8 Fake 2 0.3 1 − 0.3 = 0.7
Now take the log of each value and average:
Average the logs for the two real samples.
Average the logs for the two generated samples. Use the chance the discriminator gave to “generated.”
Add the two averages to get the score.

For the original minimax objective, the discriminator tries to push this total up toward zero. The generator tries to bring the generated-sample term down by making its outputs receive higher D values. The digit tutorial uses a different generator loss with the same practical goal.

blocks.alt: Worked example: four critic values and the totals
blocks.caption: Two real and two fake samples, step by step.

blocks.text: From the worked example to the board equations

The scorecard used two examples per source. The board writes the same calculation for any two batch sizes. The real batch contains the samples xᵢ. The generated batch comes from fresh random inputs zⱼ passed through the generator.
Divide each sum by its own batch size. This keeps both sources equally weighted in the objective even when you draw more samples from one source.
Discriminator update

Hold the generator’s settings fixed. The positive step size controls how far to move. The plus sign moves the discriminator uphill on the score, so the update is gradient ascent. This is the update shown on page 5 of the board notes.

blocks.alt: The discriminator scores both batches. Its gradient updates only its own weights.
blocks.caption: The generator produces the fake batch in the forward pass. Detaching the batch cuts the backward path to the generator.

blocks.text: Generator update in the original minimax game

Hold the discriminator settings fixed. The real batch and its scores are independent of the generator weights, so the derivative of the real term is zero. Only the generated term is needed for this update.

The minus sign moves downhill on the generator’s minimax objective. The gradient still passes through the discriminator because its score depends on the generated sample. Freezing the discriminator keeps its weights fixed while this calculation runs.

blocks.alt: Noise flows through the generator and fixed discriminator to the score. The gradient flows back through the discriminator to update the generator.
blocks.caption: The backward arrow represents a gradient through the fixed discriminator. Only the generator’s weights update.

blocks.text: Practice — trace the gradient

Question: Which weights change on the discriminator turn? Answer: Only the discriminator weights change. The generator produces the fake examples in the forward pass, and the detached examples stop the gradient from reaching the generator.

Question: Why does the generator update drop the real-data term? Answer: The real scores use the fixed discriminator and real inputs, so they have zero derivative with respect to the generator’s weights.
Taking turns
The usual way: one critic turn, then one generator turn. Repeat.
Some people do more turns for one network. For example, five generator turns for each critic turn. The right choice depends on the task.

blocks.alt: Two turns: critic goes up, generator goes down
blocks.caption: Arrows refer to the shared minimax score. Frozen weights stay fixed, but the network still runs.

blocks.text: Everyday example An art student draws fake paintings. An art teacher learns to spot them. The student then paints better fakes. The teacher learns again. After many rounds, the fakes are hard to spot.
When to stop?
Check fixed-noise samples at regular intervals. Look for recognizable digits and variety across outputs. A low training loss alone does not show that the generator has learned the range of digits.
In one line
First the critic learns to spot fakes. Then the generator learns to fool it. Repeat.
Words to remember: batch · gradient · going up · going down · frozen · taking turns
Practice — Quick check
Question: Why does the generator's turn not need real data? Answer: The real-data part of the score does not depend on the generator. So it does not change the generator's direction.
Question: In the critic's turn, which way do we move the weights? Answer: Up. We want the score to get bigger.
Question: In the critic's turn, which network is frozen? Answer: The generator.

sections.title: Tutorial — A GAN that draws digits

blocks.text: Start here You learned the idea. Now we build it in code. We will teach a GAN to draw handwritten digits, like the numbers 0 to 9.
Words you will see
• MNIST: a free set of handwritten digit pictures. Each picture is small and black and white.
• Pixel: one dot in a picture.
• Image size 28 × 28: the picture has 28 rows and 28 columns of pixels. That is 784 pixels in total.
• MLP (fully connected network): a simple neural network where every number connects to every number in the next layer.
• Layer: one step in the network.
• Activation: a simple rule applied after a layer. It bends the numbers a little. ReLU, LeakyReLU and tanh are three such rules.
• Epoch: one full pass through all the training pictures.
• Batch size: how many pictures we use at once. Here it is 128.
Step 1: prepare the pictures
• Turn each picture into numbers.
• Rescale pixels from [0, 1] to [−1, 1] by subtracting 0.5 and dividing by 0.5. The input 0 becomes −1, 0.5 becomes 0, and 1 becomes 1.
Correction to the recording. The second normalization argument is the standard deviation used as a divisor. Here it is 0.5. A variance of 0.5 would imply a different divisor.
Then we group the pictures into batches of 128, and shuffle them.
Step 2: the generator
The generator takes 100 random numbers as input. It gives back 784 numbers, which we reshape into a 28 × 28 picture.
Layer Input → output Activation 1 100 → 256 ReLU 2 256 → 512 ReLU 3 512 → 1024 ReLU 4 1024 → 784 tanh
tanh keeps the output between −1 and 1. That matches our picture numbers.

blocks.alt: 100 numbers through layers to a 28 by 28 picture
blocks.caption: From 100 random numbers to a 28 × 28 picture, layer by layer.

blocks.text: Step 3: the discriminator (the critic)
The discriminator takes 784 numbers, which is one picture. It gives back one number between 0 and 1. That number is its guess: "chance this picture is real".
Layer Input → output Activation 1 784 → 512 LeakyReLU 2 512 → 256 LeakyReLU 3 256 → 1 sigmoid
The sigmoid makes the answer a value between 0 and 1.
Step 4: the loss
The loss is a number that says how wrong the network is. Lower is better.
We use a loss called BCE. It checks a yes-or-no guess against the right answer, and gives a bigger loss when the guess is more wrong.
• For the discriminator: real pictures should get answer 1. Fake pictures should get answer 0. We add both losses.
• For the generator: fake pictures should get answer 1. The generator wants the discriminator to say "real".

blocks.alt: Noise to generator to fake picture to critic to loss
blocks.caption: One full loop of the tutorial, from noise to loss.

blocks.text: Lecture example — why the generator uses 1 During the generator update, target 1 gives a loss of −log D for generated pictures. This is the non-saturating generator loss. It rewards higher D and gives a stronger signal early in training when the discriminator confidently rejects the generated samples.
Step 5: one training round
1. Take a batch of real pictures. Ask the discriminator. Find the loss with label 1.
2. Make fake pictures from random noise. Ask the discriminator. Find the loss with label 0.
3. Add the two losses. Update only the discriminator.
4. Make new fake pictures. Ask the discriminator. Find the loss with label 1. Update only the generator.

In step 2 we use detach. Detach cuts the gradient path back to the generator while leaving the generated pictures available to the discriminator. During the generator turn, use fresh, attached outputs so the gradient can reach the generator through the fixed discriminator.
Worked example — one update in pseudocode

real = next_batch()
fake = G(sample_noise())
loss_D = BCE(D(real), 1) + BCE(D(fake.detach()), 0)
update_only(D, loss_D)

fake = G(sample_noise())
freeze_parameters(D)
loss_G = BCE(D(fake), 1)
update_only(G, loss_G)
unfreeze_parameters(D)
Freeze the discriminator parameters without disabling the calculation through the discriminator. The generator still needs that gradient.
Training modes
The tutorial tries three ways:
• 1 : 1 — one generator update, one discriminator update.
• 5 : 1 — five generator updates for each discriminator update.
• 1 : 5 — five discriminator updates for each generator update.
The number 5 is just an example. You can change it.
What to expect

The tutorial runs 50 epochs as a trial. Use the same random noise each time you check the pictures, so you can compare them fairly. Early pictures are rough. Later pictures should look more like digits. Exact outputs vary with the initialization, seed, and training settings.
Try these
1. Change the number of epochs and see how the pictures change.
2. Try the 5 : 1 and 1 : 5 modes and compare the pictures.
In one line
A simple GAN in code has two small networks, two optimizers (one per network), and a BCE loss. We train them in turns.
Words to remember: MNIST · pixel · layer · activation · epoch · batch · loss · detach
Practice — Quick check
Question: Why does the generator use tanh at the end? Answer: Because the pictures are scaled between −1 and 1, and tanh gives values in that range.
Question: What does detach do? Answer: It stops the calculation from changing the generator during the discriminator's turn.
Question: What label does the generator's fake picture get? Answer: 1. The generator wants the discriminator to say "real".
Start here Scan the tables, then trace the derivation from VDM to one round of GAN training. Finish by trying the recall questions before opening the answers.
The big picture

rows: Real data, from a source we do not know
A generator that turns random noise into fake data
Fake data that looks like the real data
Why not measure the difference directly?
We cannot compute it from samples
Estimate the critic’s lower-bound objective using separate sample averages
It finds the best way to score real vs fake
The generator makes the score small. The critic makes it big.

Fake data that looks like the real data Why not measure the difference directly? We cannot compute it from samples What do we do instead? Estimate the critic’s lower-bound objective using separate sample averages What is the critic for? It finds the best way to score real vs fake What is the final game? The generator makes the score small. The critic makes it big.
The GAN version

rows: Gives a value between 0 and 1. Close to 1 means "real".
Average of log D on real data, plus average of log(1 − D) on fake data
blocks.text: Item Simple meaning Critic (discriminator) D Gives a value between 0 and 1. Close to 1 means "real". For real data We want D close to 1 For fake data We want D close to 0 Score Average of log D on real data, plus average of log(1 − D) on fake data
Training in one table

Turn Which network changes? Which way? Which data? Critic's turn the critic up (make the score bigger) real batch and fake batch Generator's turn the generator down (make the score smaller) fake batch only
Numbers to remember
• If D = 0.5 for everything, each log is about −0.69.
• A digit picture has 28 × 28 = 784 pixels.
• Random noise size in the tutorial: 100.
• Batch size in the tutorial: 128.
• Pixel range after normalizing: −1 to 1.
Common mix-ups
• Measure and bound: improve the critic to tighten the population bound within its family. Then update the generator to reduce that score. The batch score estimates the population score.
• Raw score and discriminator probability: the raw score can be any real number. For a finite raw score, the sigmoid output lies strictly between 0 and 1.
• Going up vs going down: the critic goes up. The generator goes down.
• Why no real data for the generator: the real-data part does not depend on the generator.
Words to remember: divergence · lower bound · critic · generator · up · down · loss · detach
Trace the full derivation

Keep one picture in mind. The real coin and the computer coin each give a batch of tosses. We want the computer to match the real coin’s chances. For images, the same goal applies to the whole distribution of pictures.
1. Compare the two distributions
The real distribution is fixed. The generated distribution changes when we change the generator weights θ. The goal of VDM is to find weights that make the chosen divergence small.

We have examples from the two sources, so we use a critic to score them. The real-data average rewards the critic’s scores. The generated-data average subtracts a penalty from the conjugate. For every admissible critic, the resulting population score is a lower bound.
2. Give the critic a network

With the generator fixed, search for the best critic in the network family. Its weights w control a raw number. A divergence-specific activation converts that number to a score where the conjugate is finite.

The critic raises the score to expose a mismatch. The generator lowers it by changing the distribution it produces. The best critic in a restricted family can still give a bound below the true divergence.
3. Get the two terms of the GAN score
The board uses the following function and its conjugate. The conjugate’s log needs a positive argument, so its input t must be negative.

This choice has f(1) equal to minus twice log 2. Adding twice log 2 normalizes it to zero at 1 and adds the same constant to the objective for every choice of weights. The updates stay the same. The equations below use the board’s original choice.
Apply a sigmoid to the raw output to get the discriminator probability. Its log is negative, so it gives a valid critic score.
The real term already uses the log of D. In the generated term, exponentiating the critic score gives D back. Subtracting the conjugate leaves the log of the probability assigned to “generated.”

For a quick check, take the same D value of 0.8. A real example contributes log(0.8), about −0.223. A generated example contributes log(0.2), about −1.609. The true source determines which probability gets credit.
4. Turn the expectations into batch averages

Draw B₁ real examples and B₂ noise inputs. The generator maps each noise input to one generated example. Divide each sum by its own batch size, so both sources keep the same weight even when the batch sizes differ.
5. Take one turn for each network
First hold θ fixed. Use both batches and update the discriminator weights w. The plus sign moves uphill on the score.
Now hold w fixed. The real examples and their discriminator scores do not depend on θ. Their derivative with respect to θ is zero, so only the generated term contributes.

For the original minimax update, the minus sign moves the generator downhill on this term. The gradient travels through the fixed discriminator to reach the generator. The digit tutorial uses the non-saturating loss, which instead minimizes the negative average of log D on generated examples.

Repeat with fresh batches. If the two distributions match and the discriminator is optimal with the sources equally weighted, its output is 0.5 on the shared support. A score of 0.5 from a partly trained discriminator alone does not establish a match.
Practice — recall the derivation
Question: What is the generator trying to match? Answer: The distribution of real examples. The divergence compares that distribution with the distribution of generated examples.

Question: What does the variational score give us, and what can a restricted critic miss? Answer: It gives a population lower bound on the divergence. Even the best critic in a restricted family can leave a gap.
Question: What roles do V, the activation, and T play? Answer: V gives a raw number. The activation maps it into the allowed domain. T is the final score used in the variational objective.
Question: Why does the generated term become log(1 − D)? Answer: The GAN critic uses log D. Exponentiating gives D, and subtracting the conjugate leaves log(1 − D).
Question: What does each network want from a generated example? Answer: The discriminator wants its real probability low. The generator wants that probability high.
Question: Why divide the two sums by different denominators? Answer: Each denominator counts its own batch. Each sum becomes an average, so a larger batch does not give that source extra weight.
Question: Which update uses a plus sign and which weights change? Answer: The discriminator uses ascent on the GAN score. Only its weights w change on that turn.

Question: Why can the generator omit the real term, and where does the gradient flow? Answer: The real term is independent of θ. The generated term sends a gradient through the fixed discriminator back into the generator.
Question: When does the ideal discriminator output 0.5? Answer: When real and generated distributions match, with both sources equally weighted. This holds on their shared support.

Question: Why does the digit tutorial give generated pictures target 1 on the generator turn? Answer: The non-saturating loss uses target 1 to reward generated pictures that the discriminator scores as real.

sections.title: Detailed notes on variational divergence minimization

blocks.text: What is VDM?
Variational Divergence Minimization (VDM) is a framework for training generative models by minimizing a divergence between the real-data distribution and the model-generated distribution.
The central idea is to convert a divergence, which may be difficult to compute directly, into a variational optimization objective that can be estimated from samples.
Goal: Train a generator so that its output distribution resembles the distribution of real training data.
Dataset and real-data distribution
Consider a dataset:
Assume the observations are independently and identically distributed:
Here:
\(D\): training dataset
\(x_i\): an individual training sample
\(n\): number of samples
\(P_X\): real-data probability distribution
i.i.d.: independent and identically distributed
For example, if the dataset contains handwritten digits, \(P_X\) describes the underlying distribution of real digit images.
We observe samples from \(P_X\), but generally do not know its exact probability density.

blocks.text: Original divergence minimization objective
We want the generated distribution \(P_\theta\) to resemble the real distribution \(P_X\).
The mathematical objective is:
Here, \(D_f\) is an \(f\)-divergence.
For distributions with densities \(p_X\) and \(p_\theta\), under appropriate conditions:
The function \(f\) is convex, conventionally normalized by \(f(1)=0\).
The notation \(\arg\min_\theta\) means finding the generator parameters that minimize the divergence.
Important: The generator minimizes divergence; it does not necessarily minimize the individual output values of the scoring network.
Why direct divergence minimization is difficult
The divergence formula involves the density ratio:
In many generative modeling problems, we can sample from the real and generated distributions but cannot evaluate both densities directly.
This makes the original divergence difficult to calculate and optimize.
The solution is to use the variational representation studied in Week 1.

blocks.text: Parameterizing the scoring function
Instead of searching over all possible functions \(T\), represent the scoring function with a neural network:
where \(w\) contains the scoring network's trainable parameters.
The practical objective becomes:
The scoring network learns a function that maximizes the variational objective for a fixed generator.
Its output is a score, not necessarily a probability.
The function must also satisfy the domain requirements of \(f^*\). The teacher introduces a suitable output activation for this in the next topic.
The min–max objective
Combining generator optimization with scoring-network optimization gives:
The two networks have opposing optimization objectives.
Scoring network:
For fixed generator parameters, find the scoring function that gives the strongest available variational lower bound.
Generator:
For a fixed scoring function, update the generator to reduce the objective.
The intended overall result is to reduce the divergence between real and generated distributions.

When the scoring-function family is restricted, the maximized variational objective may be only a lower bound on the true divergence. Exact equivalence requires suitable assumptions about the function class and optimization.

blocks.alt: The scoring network maximizes the variational objective; the generator minimizes it. The displayed objective is not a rule to minimize each individual score.
blocks.caption: The scoring network maximizes the variational objective; the generator minimizes it. The displayed objective is not a rule to minimize each individual score.

blocks.text: Worked example — estimate the objective from samples
Expectations are population averages. With n real samples and m independent noise samples, replace each expectation by its own sample average. The real and generated batch sizes need not be equal.

Suppose the mean score on real samples is 1.5, and the mean conjugate-transformed score on generated samples is 0.6. The estimated objective is 1.5 − 0.6 = 0.9. These are illustrative evaluated averages, not raw probabilities.

Keep the scoring network fixed. If a generator update changes the second mean to 0.8, the estimate becomes 1.5 − 0.8 = 0.7. The objective decreased. Notice that the generated conjugate-transformed term increased: minimizing the difference does not mean pushing every scoring output down.

A finite-sample estimate fluctuates and need not itself be a certified lower bound on the population divergence. The variational lower-bound statement concerns the population expectations under its assumptions.
Why is this adversarial optimization?
The problem is called adversarial because the two networks have opposing objectives.
The scoring network tries to expose discrepancies between real and generated distributions.
The generator tries to reduce those discrepancies.
The networks do not need to output opposite numerical scores. Their opposition comes from maximizing versus minimizing the same objective.
This leads to a min–max or saddle-point optimization problem.

blocks.alt: The networks optimize the same objective in opposite directions: the critic exposes discrepancies and the generator reduces them.
blocks.caption: The networks optimize the same objective in opposite directions: the critic exposes discrepancies and the generator reduces them.

blocks.text: Complete mathematical flow

There are two sampling streams, not a transformation from real observations into latent noise. Real observations come from the dataset; latent noise enters the generator. The scoring network evaluates samples from both streams.

blocks.tex: \begin{aligned}x_i&\sim P_X &&\text{(real-data stream)}\\z_j&\sim\mathcal N(0,I),\quad \hat x_j=g_\theta(z_j)\sim P_\theta &&\text{(generated-data stream)}\end{aligned}

blocks.text: The original goal is to choose generator parameters that minimize the divergence. Its variational realization replaces the density calculation with expectations and a trainable scoring network.

We write sup when a best score may be approached without being attained. The usual min–max notation assumes the relevant extrema are attained. With a restricted neural-network family, the maximized objective can remain a lower bound rather than the full divergence.
Common mistakes
Confusing \(P_X\) and \(P_\theta\): \(P_X\) is the real-data distribution; \(P_\theta\) is the generated distribution.
Confusing \(\theta\) and \(w\): \(\theta\) belongs to the generator; \(w\) belongs to the scoring network.
Assuming the critic minimizes: The scoring network maximizes the variational objective.
Assuming the scoring output must be zero: The goal is not to force every \(T_w(x)\) to zero.
Treating a restricted variational lower bound as automatically equal to the divergence: Equality requires suitable conditions.
Confusing \(\min\) and \(\arg\min\): The former returns the minimum value; the latter identifies parameters achieving it.
Quick revision
VDM: Variational Divergence Minimization.
Real distribution: \(P_X\).
Noise: \(z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)\).
Generator: \(\hat{x}=g_\theta(z)\).
Generated distribution: \(P_\theta\).
Scoring network: \(T_w(x)\).
Generator objective: Minimize discrepancy.
Scoring network objective: Maximize the variational lower bound.
Overall objective:
One-line memory anchor:
The scoring network finds the strongest available measure of the difference, while the generator learns to reduce that difference.
Next topic: Implementing VDM with neural networks, including the output activation needed to keep \(T_w(x)\) in the domain of the convex conjugate.
Practice — check your understanding

Question: What changes when the generator parameters change? Answer: The mapping from noise to generated observations changes, so the induced distribution P_θ may change. The real-data distribution P_X is the target and is not trained by those updates.

Question: Which network maximizes the objective? Answer: The scoring network, with parameters w, maximizes it while the generator is fixed. The generator, with parameters θ, minimizes it while the scoring network is fixed.

Question: Does the scoring network output a probability by definition? Answer: No. It outputs an admissible score. Its permitted output range depends on the effective domain of the chosen convex conjugate.

Question: Is every neural scoring network guaranteed to recover the exact divergence? Answer: No. A restricted function family and imperfect optimization may leave a gap. Equality requires a sufficiently rich admissible class and suitable regularity assumptions.

Question: Real mean score = 2.0 and generated mean conjugate-transformed score = 1.3. What is the estimated objective? Answer: 2.0 − 1.3 = 0.7. The second term is the average after applying the convex conjugate, not necessarily the average raw critic score.
Question: In the saddle example, what happens along θ when w = 0? Answer: The objective is θ², minimized at θ = 0. Along w with θ = 0, it is −w², maximized at w = 0.

Question: Are real samples generated by passing them through the noise distribution? Answer: No. Real samples and latent noise are separate inputs. Noise passes through the generator to produce synthetic samples; the scoring network can evaluate both real and synthetic samples.

Question: What is the difference between min and argmin? Answer: min gives the smallest objective value; argmin gives the parameter value or set of values that achieves that value. An optimum need not always be attained.
